title: A deployment declaration is one every reader reads the same way, or refuses
intent: An app's deployment declaration is read by its own gate and by tools that drive a deploy without ever importing the app, so a file one of them reads one way and another reads differently is a deploy nobody described. It must parse as one object, validate against deployment-declaration.schema.json, and sit in exactly one state: units with how they are built, or opted out with a reason that is not blank. Units without a build, or an opt-out beside a build, are refused rather than guessed into a state. A key the vocabulary does not have is refused rather than ignored, because a misspelt stateful mark would otherwise be a backup policy that silently does nothing; a key beginning with a dollar sign is an annotation and is exempt. A key for deploy policy - who may publish, how many approvals a deploy needs, who may reach a deployed app, which gate policy applies - is refused with its own message, saying it belongs to the deploying tool's environment policy and not to this file: anyone who can commit to the app could lower a policy kept here, the schema names those keys so every reader says the same, and the opted-out state can never carry one. A schema version, a closed-vocabulary value, or a datastore kind and version the reader's stack cannot honour is refused by name, never treated as a nearby one. There is no free image field, so the file cannot name a registry; a command is an argument list, never a shell string; every string has a length cap and refuses control characters. Every path the file leads a reader to - the profile, its overrides, and the build contexts and build files of the units it declares - is resolved against the checkout, links followed, and refused when it lands outside; and the profile it names is never the development one. The file must also agree with itself: no two units or volumes share an id, a unit's size names an entry of the size table, a backup policy sits only on a unit declared stateful, and a backup left to its owner appears only on a database the deployment does not run. The words only a generator reads stand only in the generated state, and a system package one of them names is one the stack's closed table carries, so a stack whose table is empty refuses every name; a volume's mount names declared units and a path inside the app's var directory that cannot climb out of it, and in the generated state every volume says where it is mounted. An absent file is undeclared and passes. Each refusal names the field and the values it allows.
reference: deployment.json at the project root, the document deployment-declaration.schema.json describes; terp verify --only deployment runs this check from files alone, without importing the app, and terp-arch carries a byte-for-byte copy of the schema held equal to the pinned spec release. deployment-declaration.fixtures.json names the field and the allowed values for every violation case, and describes the path escapes a corpus case cannot carry (a symbolic link, a work tree) as trees a reader's test builds. The checkout is the root of the git work tree holding the project root, else the project root; the development profile is the compose file workbench.json names, else docker-compose.yml at the project root, and no file-name infix is required of the deployment one. The datastore table is the one the framework release publishes, one digest per kind and version (a corpus case that names a kind carries it as datastore-table.json). build: generated is read as a declared state like own; whether its build files are the generator's render is deployment_generated_files_match_their_render's question, which terp verify --only generated asks. A toolchain with no generator refuses generated by name: "this toolchain cannot honour generated; upgrade, or declare own". The system-package table is the one the framework release publishes (empty in this release, so every name is refused; a corpus case that names a package carries it as system-package-table.json, {"packages": {}}), and a generator block beside build own is refused at generator. A deploy-policy key is refused with "<key> is deploy policy: it belongs to the deploying tool's environment policy, not to this file".
escape: Declare the opted-out state: replace the whole file with unmanaged set to true and a reason that says why. The check is then off, and a tool that drives deploys reports that reason instead of driving the app. The opted-out state carries nothing else, so it can never carry deploy policy.

runtime.rationale: The declaration is a checked-in file the running app never reads: nothing in it reaches the process, so no runtime seam of the app can hold it. Its other readers - the tools that drive a deploy - read it again as data with their own fail-closed readers, which are those tools' controls, not the app's runtime.
